screens.title: Automating Operations with SSM Run Command and Automation Documents
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we learn two complementary automation tools in Systems Manager. First, Run Command gives you secure, ad-hoc execution across many managed instances without SSH. You use command documents like AWS-RunShellScript to run a quick disk check or restart services across a tagged group of servers. Second, Automation Documents let you author YAML or JSON playbooks that define multi-step operations—create an AMI, patch, validate, and optionally roll back. You will see concrete examples of both: a single-step command for checks and a reusable Automation Document that restarts a service or installs Nginx. We also cover parameters and outputs so documents are dynamic, and essential safety controls like MaxConcurrency and ErrorThreshold to avoid widespread disruptions. By the end, you will understand when to use Run Command versus an Automation Document, how to design idempotent steps, and how to test and roll out changes safely. Think of Run Command for quick fixes and Automation Documents for repeatable, auditable operational workflows. What routine operation in your environment could you automate first?

screens.title: SSM Run Command — definition and use cases
screens.narratorSegment: Run Command is a Systems Manager feature for executing ad-hoc scripts or commands on one or many managed instances without SSH. It uses a command document—either a pre-defined document such as AWS-RunShellScript for Linux or a custom document you author—to instruct the SSM agent on each instance what to run. A practical use case is checking disk space across all web servers: instead of logging into machines one-by-one, you run a single command targeting instances by tag. Another common use is restarting a service after deployment. Run Command returns consolidated stdout and stderr so you can inspect results centrally. A common misconception is that Run Command replaces Automation Documents; it does not. Run Command is best for immediate, single-step tasks. If you need multi-step orchestration, conditional logic, or outputs for later steps, use an Automation Document. Example: use AWS-RunShellScript with commands like df -h or sudo systemctl restart myservice on a tagged group. Before running, verify the SSM agent IAM permissions and test scripts in a staging environment. How might you use Run Command during an incident? SSM Run Command — definition and use cases means run command runs scripts securely at scale for immediate operational tasks; use it for single-step needs and quick diagnostics.. In practical terms, secure ad-hoc execution across managed instances. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Run Command — definition
Core Concept

Run Command

Run immediate commands on managed instances using prebuilt or custom command documents. Results are aggregated for inspection.

Common uses
  • Check disk space across web servers
  • Restart a service after deployment
  • Install a package quickly on a few instances
Common mistake
Running broad commands without limiting targets or concurrency risks unintended impact; always test and scope targets.
Key Takeaway

Use Run Command for quick, single-step operations and centralized output; preserve Automation Documents for multi-step orchestration.

Example: check disk and restart a service
# Command Document: AWS-RunShellScript
# Commands sent to SSM agent on each instance
Commands:
  - df -h
  - sudo systemctl restart myservice
Targeting
Use tags, resource groups or instance IDs to scope execution.
Permissions
Ensure the SSM agent role has required permissions or commands will fail.
Check your understanding
When would you prefer Run Command over an Automation Document? Think of a short incident response example.

screens.title: Command Documents — pre-defined vs custom
screens.narratorSegment: Command documents are the instructions Run Command uses. AWS provides many pre-defined documents such as AWS-RunShellScript for Linux and AWS-RunPowerShellScript for Windows, plus documents that perform specific tasks like installing applications or configuring updates. These are convenient because they encapsulate common operations and reduce duplication. However, pre-defined documents may not express your exact workflow. Custom command documents let you include bespoke scripts and specific flags that match your environment. A common misconception is that custom documents are always safer. In fact, custom documents require careful testing and correct IAM permissions for the SSM agent. Use pre-defined documents to accelerate standard tasks and create custom documents when you need environment-specific logic. As a concrete example, use AWS-RunShellScript to run df -h across a tagged group for a quick health check, but author a custom document when you must perform a unique series of package manager commands with tuned retries. Always test any custom document in staging and validate outputs before broad execution. screens.title: Targeting instances for execution
screens.narratorSegment: Targeting determines which instances receive a Run Command or Automation Document execution. You can target specific instance IDs when you need isolated actions, tags when you want a group like Environment:Production and Role:WebServer, or resource groups when you have logical collections. Targeting by tag is powerful because you can add or remove instances from the group without changing the document. A practical example: to update a package on all production web servers, target instances with tags Environment:Production and Role:WebServer. Start with a dry run or a small test subset of instances to verify behavior. A frequent mistake is targeting overly broad tag values that match unintended instances; always validate your tag filters. Another common pitfall is forgetting to include newly launched instances in the appropriate PatchGroup or tag; automation then misses them. As a safeguard, include a verification step at the end of your Automation Document to confirm the intended instances processed successfully and emit an output listing instance IDs that failed, making diagnosis straightforward. How will you validate your target set before a broad rollout? Targeting instances for execution means choose instance ids for precision, tags for flexible groups, and resource groups for logical collections; always validate target filters before execution.. In practical terms, selecting the right scope: instance ids, tags, or resource groups. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Targeting instances
Process Flow

Target selection steps

  1. Identify scope: decide if this is one instance, a role, or environment-wide.
  2. Choose target type: instance IDs for precision, tags for groups, or resource groups for logical sets.
  3. Run on a small test subset first to verify commands and permissions.
  4. Review outputs and logs; if successful, expand concurrency and scope as needed.
Pro tip
Tag hygiene is critical. Consistent tagging prevents accidental broad changes and makes patch groups reliable.
Concrete scenario
You need to update a package on production web servers. Define a tag filter Environment:Production and Role:WebServer, test on two instances, then run with MaxConcurrency configured to limit blast radius.
Validation
Include a final verification step that curls localhost or checks a service status and emits an output.
Common mistake
Assuming newly launched instances inherit tags immediately; confirm tag propagation and membership in patch groups.

screens.title: Automation Document example: restart a service
screens.narratorSegment: Automation Documents are YAML or JSON playbooks that orchestrate a series of steps across AWS resources. Each document contains parameters for inputs, mainSteps that define actions, and optional outputs selectors. Here we walk through a practical restart-service document provided in the chapter. The document accepts an InstanceId and ServiceName, stops the service, starts it again, then checks status and returns the stdout as an output named ServiceStatus. Notice the use of onFailure policies: stopService and startService are marked to Abort on failure, while checkServiceStatus continues so you can still capture output even if the status check fails. A key point is that outputs allow downstream automation or a human operator to inspect results and decide on rollback. A common misconception is that Automation Documents always succeed; they do not. Use onFailure settings purposefully and include rollback steps or AMI creation if you need safe restore points. keyIdea.text: Parameters, mainSteps with actions and onFailure policies, and outputs form the core of an Automation Document for orchestration and observability.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Automation Document — example
Document (YAML)
description: "Restarts a specified service on an EC2 instance."
schemaVersion: "0.3"
parameters:
  InstanceId:
    type: String
  ServiceName:
    type: String
mainSteps:
  - name: stopService
    action: aws:runShellScript
    inputs:
      InstanceIds: ["{{ InstanceId }}"]
      Commands: ["sudo systemctl stop {{ ServiceName }}"]
    onFailure: Abort
  - name: startService
    action: aws:runShellScript
    inputs:
      InstanceIds: ["{{ InstanceId }}"]
      Commands: ["sudo systemctl start {{ ServiceName }}"]
    onFailure: Abort
  - name: checkServiceStatus
    action: aws:runShellScript
    inputs:
      InstanceIds: ["{{ InstanceId }}"]
      Commands: ["sudo systemctl status {{ ServiceName }} --no-pager"]
    outputs:
      - Name: ServiceStatus
        Selector: "$.stdout"
        Type: String
    onFailure: Continue
Annotations
Parameters: Inputs make this document reusable across instances and services.
onFailure: Controls whether orchestration aborts or continues on step failure.
Outputs: Capture stdout for validation or downstream decisions.
Misconception

Continuing on failure without appropriate checks may hide issues; prefer explicit validation steps and rollback when needed.

screens.title: Patching workflow example with Automation Documents
screens.narratorSegment: Patching an application server is a canonical use for Automation Documents. A safe, repeatable workflow contains these steps: create an AMI for rollback, stop the application service, apply OS patches, restart the service, verify application health, and then either delete the temporary AMI if successful or roll back to the AMI if verification fails. Each step becomes a mainStep in a document with clear onFailure policies. For example, snapshot creation should Abort on failure because you want a rollback point before making changes. Verification should capture outputs so you can decide whether to continue or restore. Parameters let you target a single InstanceId or a PatchGroup so the same document can be reused across many servers. A common mistake is skipping AMI creation and relying only on manual notes; that increases recovery time if a patch breaks the app. Practice this workflow in staging and test rollback paths. After a successful test, schedule the Automation Document or trigger it manually with controlled concurrency. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Patching workflow
Process

Patch an application server

Step 1 — Create AMI
Take an image as a rollback point. Abort if this fails.
Step 2 — Stop service
Stop application processes cleanly before patching.
Step 3 — Apply patches
Run package updates with timeouts and retries where appropriate.
Step 4 — Restart and verify
Restart service and perform health checks; capture outputs for decision logic.
Step 5 — Conditional cleanup or rollback
Delete the AMI if successful; otherwise, restore from AMI.
Example decision rule
If the health check output contains an expected status, continue to cleanup. If failures exceed a threshold, trigger rollback to the AMI and alert operators.
Why it matters
This pattern reduces downtime and gives you a fast recovery point if a patch causes a regression.

screens.title: Parameters and Outputs in Automation Documents
screens.narratorSegment: Parameters and outputs are the mechanisms that make Automation Documents flexible and observable. Parameters act as inputs you pass at execution time—common examples are InstanceId or PatchGroup. By defining parameters, a single document can target different instances or environments without modification. Outputs capture results from steps, typically by selecting an element from a step's JSON result, like the standard output of a shell script. You might capture a curl response or the stdout of a service status check and name it ServiceStatus. That output can drive conditional logic or be recorded for audit. A useful mistake to avoid is hardcoding instance identifiers in documents; parameters prevent that and make documents reusable. Also, ensure your outputs use selectors that map to the exact JSON path your action returns. As a practice, include a verification step that emits a clear output and have the automation either continue, abort, or rollback depending on that output. How would you use an output to gate a rollback? screens.title: Rate control: MaxConcurrency and ErrorThreshold
screens.narratorSegment: When executing commands across many instances you must control pace and failure tolerance. MaxConcurrency limits how many instances run a command at the same time; ErrorThreshold sets how many failures are permitted before halting remaining execution. For example, to patch 100 instances and ensure at most 10 patch at once while stopping the run if 5 fail, set MaxConcurrency to 10 and ErrorThreshold to 5. Start conservatively in production and increase concurrency once you validate outcomes. A common mistake is setting High concurrency and a high error threshold; that can propagate a bad change quickly. Another pitfall is misunderstanding percentage syntax—MaxConcurrency may accept an absolute number or a percentage, and percent values change behavior as the fleet grows. Combine rate control with staged targeting (small canary group then broader rollout) and always have clear rollback steps. Use these controls in both Run Command executions and Automation Document executions when steps run across many instances. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › InstallNginxAutomation Lab
Step-by-step
  1. Create IAM role for Automation and attach AmazonSSMAutomationRole policy.
  2. Open Systems Manager Automation and create a new YAML document.
  3. Paste the InstallNginxAutomation YAML and save with a name like InstallNginxAutomation.
  4. Execute the document, select the automation role, pass InstanceId, and run.
  5. Monitor steps and review the verify step output for a successful curl response.
Safety note
If you open port 80 to verify the welcome page, close it immediately after verification.
Document snippet
description: "Installs Nginx on a specified EC2 instance."
schemaVersion: "0.3"
parameters:
  InstanceId:
    type: String
mainSteps:
  - name: installNginx
    action: aws:runShellScript
    inputs:
      InstanceIds: ["{{ InstanceId }}"]
      Commands:
        - "sudo yum update -y"
        - "sudo amazon-linux-extras install nginx1 -y"
        - "sudo systemctl enable nginx"
        - "sudo systemctl start nginx"
  - name: verifyNginx
    action: aws:runShellScript
    inputs:
      InstanceIds: ["{{ InstanceId }}"]
      Commands: ["curl -I localhost"]
    outputs:
      - Name: NginxStatus
        Selector: "$.stdout"
        Type: String

screens.title: Idempotency, testing, and rollout patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Idempotency means an operation yields the same result when executed multiple times. For automation this is crucial: retries, orchestration replays, or scheduled runs should not produce unintended side effects. Make installation steps check for existing state before changing it—for example, only install a package if it is absent, or use systemctl to check service state before starting it. Testing complements idempotency: validate documents in a staging environment and include verification steps that expose outputs. Rollout patterns matter too: start with a small canary group, observe metrics and logs, then progressively increase scope with higher concurrency if results are healthy. Use MaxConcurrency and ErrorThreshold together with staged targeting to minimize blast radius. A common misconception is that a successful test once guarantees production safety; in reality, differences in configuration, scale, and traffic can reveal issues—so run multiple canaries and monitor closely. Finally, embed cleanup and rollback steps in your Automation Documents so recovery is automated as well. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we learn two complementary automation tools in Systems Manager. First, Run Command gives you secure, ad-hoc execution across many managed instances without SSH. You use command documents like AWS-RunShellScript to run a quick disk check or restart services across a tagged group of servers. Second, Automation Documents let you author YAML or JSON playbooks that define multi-step operations—create an AMI, patch, validate, and optionally roll back. You will see concrete examples of both: a single-step command for checks and a reusable Automation Document that restarts a service or installs Nginx. We also cover parameters and outputs so documents are dynamic, and essential safety controls like MaxConcurrency and ErrorThreshold to avoid widespread disruptions. By the end, you will understand when to use Run Command versus an Automation Document, how to design idempotent steps, and how to test and roll out changes safely. Think of Run Command for quick fixes and Automation Documents for repeatable, auditable operational workflows. What routine operation in your environment could you automate first?

By the end of this chapter you will execute and design automated operations reliably. First, you will run ad-hoc commands across a fleet using Systems Manager Run Command, selecting targets by instance IDs, tags, or resource groups so you avoid manual SSH and reduce incident response time. Second, you will author Automation Documents—YAML or JSON playbooks—with parameters, outputs, and step-level onFailure policies so complex operations become repeatable and auditable. These skills let you codify routine maintenance, patching, and incident response. You will also learn to use parameters and outputs to make documents dynamic, enabling the same playbook to work across different instances or environments. Finally, you will apply rate controls and error thresholds to avoid large-scale outages when executing across many instances. Each objective includes a small practical mnemonic and a verified competency milestone so you know when you’re ready to use these techniques in production.

These supporting objectives focus on targeting, idempotency, and testing—skills essential to using Run Command and Automation Documents in production. You will learn how to target instances using tags, resource groups, or explicit instance IDs so changes reach the intended machines. You will also practice making steps idempotent; that is, designing commands so they produce the same result if run more than once. Idempotency reduces risk when retries occur or when Automation Documents run frequently. Finally, you will validate and test scripts in a non-production environment, and learn common troubleshooting checks such as verifying IAM permissions for the SSM agent and checking script syntax. Each objective maps to a small mnemonic or test you can run during the hands-on activity to verify your competency before scaling to production. Learning Objectives — Practical Skills means target precisely, design idempotent steps, and test thoroughly so automation is safe and repeatable.. In practical terms, supporting skills you'll apply in the lab and on the job. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Run Command is a Systems Manager feature for executing ad-hoc scripts or commands on one or many managed instances without SSH. It uses a command document—either a pre-defined document such as AWS-RunShellScript for Linux or a custom document you author—to instruct the SSM agent on each instance what to run. A practical use case is checking disk space across all web servers: instead of logging into machines one-by-one, you run a single command targeting instances by tag. Another common use is restarting a service after deployment. Run Command returns consolidated stdout and stderr so you can inspect results centrally. A common misconception is that Run Command replaces Automation Documents; it does not. Run Command is best for immediate, single-step tasks. If you need multi-step orchestration, conditional logic, or outputs for later steps, use an Automation Document. Idempotency means an operation yields the same result when executed multiple times. For automation this is crucial: retries, orchestration replays, or scheduled runs should not produce unintended side effects.
